statements.quote: In the **Minimal Neuron** section, we saw that one neuron does something very simple: it multiplies its input by a weight, adds a bias, and then bends the result with an activation function.
statements.section: From a Single Neuron to a Deep Network

statements.quote: A single neuron can draw *one* straight line through data, and nothing more.
statements.section: From a Single Neuron to a Deep Network

statements.quote: **Deep Learning** — a term first used in a different context by \citeauthor{deeplearningfirstuse} (\citeyear{deeplearningfirstuse}), reintroduced for neural networks by \citeauthor{aizenberg2000}, and popularized after \citeauthor{hinton2006} — is what happens when we stop using one neuron and start **stacking many of them in layers**, feeding the output of one layer as the input to the next.
statements.section: From a Single Neuron to a Deep Network

statements.quote: A single layer takes a vector of inputs $\mathbf{x}$ and produces a vector of outputs $\mathbf{h}$ (called a *hidden state*, because it sits between the input and the final answer):
statements.section: One Layer at a Time

statements.quote: Reading this from the inside out:
statements.section: One Layer at a Time

statements.quote: - $W$ is a **matrix of weights**.
statements.section: One Layer at a Time

statements.quote: Each row is like one neuron's weights, and stacking many neurons side by side gives us a matrix instead of a single number.
statements.section: One Layer at a Time

statements.quote: Multiplying by $W$ mixes the inputs together in many different learned combinations at once.
statements.section: One Layer at a Time

statements.quote: - $\mathbf{b}$ is a **bias vector**, one offset per neuron.
statements.section: One Layer at a Time

statements.quote: - $\sigma$ is the **activation function** (the "bend"), applied to each entry.
statements.section: One Layer at a Time

statements.quote: Nothing exotic — just a matrix multiplication, an addition, and a bend.
statements.section: One Layer at a Time

statements.quote: "Deep" simply means: the output of one layer becomes the input of the next.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: In math, this is called **function composition**.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: Each layer has its own weights $W_n$ and biases $\mathbf{b}_n$.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: This stacking is what lets the network build a **ladder of features**: layer 1 might pick up simple things (edges, basic patterns), layer 2 combines those into shapes, and deeper layers combine those into full concepts (a face, a word, a chess position).
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: There is a beautiful mathematical guarantee behind all of this, called the **Universal Approximation Theorem**.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: It's actually a *family* of related results — notably \citeauthor{cybenko1989} (\citeyear{cybenko1989}) and \citeauthor{hornik1989universal} (\citeyear{hornik1989universal}) — and they all say roughly the same thing:
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: > A network with just **one hidden layer** can approximate **any reasonable continuous function** as closely as you want, as long as it has enough neurons.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: Formally, such a network computes:
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: which is just: take $n$ neurons, each one bends the input its own way ($\psi$ with weights $a_j$ and threshold $\theta_j$), then add up their outputs weighted by $\beta_j$.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: If $n$ is large enough, this sum can match the shape of *any* well-behaved function.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: **Two important caveats**, because this theorem is often oversold:
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: It's an **existence** proof, not a **learning** proof.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: It says the right weights *exist*, not that gradient descent will find them.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: "Enough neurons" can mean *astronomically* many.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: In practice, a shallow-but-huge network is almost never the right choice — **depth is dramatically more efficient** than width, as we'll see next.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: And the cleanest modern characterization, \citeauthor{petersen2024mathdl} (\citeyear{petersen2024mathdl}), gives an exact *if and only if*: the one-hidden-layer network is a universal approximator **if and only if** the activation is not a polynomial.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: That means sigmoid, ReLU, tanh, SiLU — every standard activation — qualifies, while no amount of width can compensate for a polynomial activation.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: So the theorem is foundational, but it doesn't explain *why* deep networks work so well.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: For that, we need to look at what depth actually buys us.
statements.section: Stacking Layers = Function Composition

statements.quote: Here's the honest, mechanical answer to why "a big pile of matrix multiplications" ends up being able to translate languages, recognize faces, and play chess better than any human.
statements.section: Why Deep Learning Works (And Why It Works *So* Well)

statements.quote: It comes down to four ingredients working together: **depth**, **nonlinearity**, **backpropagation**, and the **optimizer's hidden preferences**.
statements.section: Why Deep Learning Works (And Why It Works *So* Well)

statements.quote: A deep network is a **composition of many simple functions**.
statements.section: The One-Paragraph Answer

statements.quote: Each function (a "layer") is a matrix multiplication followed by a small bend.
statements.section: The One-Paragraph Answer

statements.quote: On its own, one layer is powerless — it can only mix, rotate, and scale.
statements.section: The One-Paragraph Answer

statements.quote: But **chained together, simple steps stack into arbitrarily complex ones**.
statements.section: The One-Paragraph Answer

statements.quote: Then **training** (forward pass → measure error → **backprop** → **optimizer step**) tunes the weights until the whole composition implements the right input-to-output map.
statements.section: The One-Paragraph Answer

statements.quote: The "storage" of knowledge is nothing more than the final tuned weights.
statements.section: The One-Paragraph Answer

statements.quote: Depth gives us **expressivity**, the nonlinearity prevents **collapse**, backprop provides an **efficient learning signal**, and the optimizer has a built-in **bias toward simple, generalizing solutions** rather than memorization.
statements.section: The One-Paragraph Answer

statements.quote: A deep network with $L$ layers just feeds each layer's output into the next:
statements.section: Depth = Composition, and Why the "Bend" Is Everything

statements.quote: **Here's the crucial part.** If you removed the bend $\sigma$, the whole stack collapses:
statements.section: Depth = Composition, and Why the "Bend" Is Everything

statements.quote: A stack of pure linear layers is **mathematically identical to one linear layer**.
statements.section: Depth = Composition, and Why the "Bend" Is Everything

statements.quote: No matter how deep, it can only draw straight lines.
statements.section: Depth = Composition, and Why the "Bend" Is Everything

statements.quote: It cannot compute $x^2$, it cannot solve XOR, it cannot tell a cat from a dog.
statements.section: Depth = Composition, and Why the "Bend" Is Everything

statements.quote: The nonlinearity **prevents that collapse**.
statements.section: Depth = Composition, and Why the "Bend" Is Everything

statements.quote: Each $\sigma$ re-bends the space, so the next matrix multiplies something that has *already been transformed*.
statements.section: Depth = Composition, and Why the "Bend" Is Everything

statements.quote: Depth alone isn't the power — **depth with a bend in between** is.
statements.section: Depth = Composition, and Why the "Bend" Is Everything

statements.quote: The mechanical reason depth is so effective is **reuse**.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: A sub-result computed by an early layer is reused by everything downstream.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: Depth turns "compute, throw away, recompute" into "compute once, reuse everywhere."
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: **A concrete example.** Suppose we want to check "is a point inside an $n$-dimensional unit box?" — meaning each coordinate must be in $(0,1)$.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: - A **shallow** (2-layer) network needs roughly $2^n$ neurons to capture this — **exponential** growth.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: - A **deep** network with $n$ layers of just a few neurons each does it in $O(n)$ total neurons.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: Each layer checks one coordinate and multiplies by the running result from the previous layer.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: This isn't a fluke: \citeauthor{telgarsky2016wars} proved there exist functions a deep net represents with $O(n)$ neurons that a shallow net needs $2^{\Omega(n)}$ neurons to match.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: And \citeauthor{montufar2014regions} showed that the number of distinct "linear regions" a ReLU network can carve out **grows exponentially with depth** — the compositional structure is exactly what buys the exponential expressivity.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: And the bound is **tight**: a depth-$L$ ReLU network of width 2 produces a "sawtooth" with exactly $2^L$ linear regions, so the exponential growth is guaranteed, not merely possible \cite{petersen2024mathdl}.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: **What this looks like conceptually:** each layer builds features **on top of** the previous layer's features.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: - Layer 1: edges, simple patterns.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: - Layer 2: patterns *made of* layer-1 patterns (corners, textures).
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: - Layer $k$: patterns made of $(k{-}1)$-level patterns.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: This matches how **the real world is structured**: pixels → edges → parts → objects; sounds → phonemes → words → meaning.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: Deep networks are compact for the same reason: the world itself is compositional.
statements.section: Why Depth Beats Width: Reuse

statements.quote: Before training, the weights are random and the network's output is garbage.
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: Forward pass** — run input $x$ through all layers, get prediction $\hat{y}$.
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: Loss** — measure how wrong we were in a single number:
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: Backpropagation** — figure out, for every single weight, "if I nudge it slightly, does the error go up or down?" Because the network is a composition, the influence of a weight in layer $\ell$ flows through *every layer after it*.
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: The **chain rule** from calculus handles this:
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: The clever part is that backprop **reuses intermediate results**, walking the error signal *backward* through the network.
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: What would naively be exponential bookkeeping becomes **linear in the number of layers**.
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: Optimizer step** — nudge every weight a small amount in the direction that reduces the error:
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: Repeat millions of times.
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: The **trajectory of the weights through weight-space** is literally what writes the knowledge into the matrices.
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: There is no separate memory — the knowledge *is* the final numbers.
statements.section: How the Knowledge Gets Into the Weights

statements.quote: There's a practical problem with stacking many layers.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: When backprop sends the error signal backward through, say, 100 layers, it gets multiplied by many small numbers along the way.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: The signal often **shrinks to nearly zero** (the "vanishing gradient" problem) or occasionally explodes.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: Early layers stop learning because they receive no meaningful feedback.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: \citeauthor{he2015resnet} introduced a stunningly simple fix: the **residual connection** (also called a skip connection).
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: Instead of each layer computing an entirely new representation, it computes just a **correction** and adds it to the running state:
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: This one change transforms deep networks in three ways:
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: Gradients flow freely.** Because of the $+h_{\ell-1}$ term, the derivative through the skip path is exactly $1$.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: The error signal has a **highway back to the earliest layers** — it can no longer be strangled by many small multiplications.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: This is what makes training networks with hundreds or even thousands of layers actually possible.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: Each layer only has to learn a small refinement.** Instead of every layer needing to reinvent the entire representation, layers are free to add tiny, targeted adjustments.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: If a layer has nothing useful to add, it can just learn $f_\ell \approx 0$ and let the input pass through unchanged.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: Bad layers become harmless; good layers become powerful.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: It creates the "residual stream."** In modern transformers, this idea becomes central: the recursively updated state $h_\ell = h_0 + \sum_{i=1}^{\ell} f_i(h_{i-1})$ acts like a **shared communication bus** that every layer can read from and write to.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: Attention heads and MLPs across the whole network exchange information by adding features into this stream and reading them out later.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: This is why transformer analyses (see \citeauthor{elhage2021framework}) treat the residual stream as the central object of the network — it's the substrate on which computation actually happens.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: Residual connections also **flatten the loss landscape** \cite[Li et al.]{li2018losslandscape}, making the optimization problem itself easier and pushing training toward solutions that generalize better.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: It's one of the rare tricks in deep learning that improves trainability, generalization, *and* interpretability all at once.
statements.section: Residual Connections: How We Actually Train *Really* Deep Networks

statements.quote: The loss $\mathcal{L}(W)$ is a surface in a space with **millions or billions of dimensions**.
statements.section: The Loss Landscape and the "Implicit Bias" That Makes It Work

statements.quote: Gradient descent is a ball rolling downhill on this surface.
statements.section: The Loss Landscape and the "Implicit Bias" That Makes It Work

statements.quote: Two facts shape what it finds.
statements.section: The Loss Landscape and the "Implicit Bias" That Makes It Work

statements.quote: **Saddle points, not local minima, are the real obstacle.** In very high dimensions, almost every flat spot is a saddle (curving up in some directions, down in others), not a true trap \cite[Dauphin et al.]{dauphin2014saddle}.
statements.section: The Loss Landscape and the "Implicit Bias" That Makes It Work

statements.quote: The **randomness in mini-batch training** acts like little kicks that knock the ball off saddles, which is why training huge networks actually works.
statements.section: The Loss Landscape and the "Implicit Bias" That Makes It Work

statements.quote: And for a single-hidden-layer network with at least as many neurons as training samples, the loss landscape has **no spurious valleys at all** — every local minimum is a global minimum \cite{petersen2024mathdl}.
statements.section: The Loss Landscape and the "Implicit Bias" That Makes It Work

statements.quote: All of these obstacles (saddles, ill-conditioning, ill-chosen learning rates) are exactly what the modern optimizer zoo was built to handle.
statements.section: The Loss Landscape and the "Implicit Bias" That Makes It Work

statements.section: The Loss Landscape and the "Implicit Bias" That Makes It Work

statements.section: The Loss Landscape and the "Implicit Bias" That Makes It Work

statements.quote: The activation function $\sigma$ (like **ReLU** or **Sigmoid**) is the glue that makes stacking work.
statements.section: The Role of Non-Linearity

statements.quote: Without it, the whole network — no matter how deep — collapses into a single linear function, because "a linear function of a linear function is still linear."
statements.section: The Role of Non-Linearity

statements.quote: By keeping non-linear "bends" between the stacks, the network can warp the coordinate space in complex ways, letting it solve problems that no straight line ever could — like the classic **XOR** gate.
statements.section: The Role of Non-Linearity
